coverage_note: Twelve items met the editorial threshold before discovery reached its ten-query ceiling; inaccessible and weaker candidates were omitted.

items.title: Disclosure of a potential medical-practice sale defeated a post-divorce fraud claim
items.publisher: New York State Unified Court System
items.summary: New York’s Fourth Department affirmed dismissal of a former wife’s effort to rescind part of a divorce settlement after her husband’s medical practice announced a sale one day after judgment. The court held that his lawyer had disclosed a potential transaction and that she waived further discovery, defeating fraudulent-omission and justifiable-reliance theories. The ruling turns on the record’s particular disclosure and waiver, not a general permission to conceal pending asset sales.

items.title: Fourth Department upholds murder conviction after rejecting a justification defense
items.publisher: New York State Unified Court System
items.summary: New York’s Fourth Department affirmed murder and weapons convictions arising from a dispute in which the defendant fired, turned back, and fired again, killing a man in his own group. The court held that the jury could reject justification because the opposing man was not using or attempting deadly force and the defendant had an opportunity to retreat. Several additional arguments were unpreserved; a suppression challenge was academic because the statements were not introduced.

items.title: Westchester court temporarily clears a football player for a fifth NCAA season
items.publisher: New York State Unified Court System
items.summary: A Westchester County Supreme Court justice granted a preliminary injunction allowing a college football player to compete in 2026–27. Reading NCAA Bylaw 12.6, the court found a likelihood that he remained eligible and that guidance excluding his 2022 cohort lacked a demonstrated rulemaking basis, appearing arbitrary and capricious. The order also blocks related sanctions and NIL interference. It preserves one season while litigation continues; it is not a final merits judgment.

items.title: AI training improved Peruvian teachers’ prompting judgment, but did not save time
items.summary: A randomized trial involving 1,269 sixth-grade teachers in 390 Lima public schools paired one day of training with a Copilot license and eight months of light-touch support. Adoption rose sharply, and treated teachers produced better prompts and were less likely to accept inadequate AI output. Yet seven measured teaching tasks showed precisely estimated null effects on time use. The working paper does not yet establish whether the intervention improved student learning.

items.title: A cross-country model puts a large price on Saudi Arabia’s learning gap
items.summary: Using data from 97 countries for 2000–19, a working paper models how harmonized learning outcomes relate to economic growth after accounting for factors including resource income. It estimates that a 180-point improvement to match top-performing systems could lift Saudi GDP by as much as 27 percent after 20 years, or $225 billion in 2021 prices. These are simulated gains under demanding assumptions, not observed effects or a forecast.

items.title: Low-cost inputs and Chinese investment helped Vietnam become a solar-panel exporter
items.summary: A working paper links firm-to-firm trade data with Vietnam’s enterprise survey for 2018–22. Inputs from subsidizing countries were about 30 percent cheaper, and Chinese inputs 50 percent cheaper; Chinese-owned firms supplied roughly three-quarters of solar exports and half of producer employment. Domestic suppliers connected to those firms also showed productivity gains. The evidence maps prices, ownership, and spillovers, but the observational comparisons do not prove that every difference was caused by subsidies or FDI.

items.title: South African coal workers face transition costs worth years of average wages
items.summary: A technical brief estimates one-time transition frictions equal to 0.70–4.59 years of average national wages for coal miners and 0.12–3.74 years for electricity workers. Workers changing sectors may also lose 29–57 percent and 37–61 percent of annual wages, respectively. These are model-based estimates inferred from job flows and wage gaps, not direct compensation claims; the calculation also excludes amenities such as health and working conditions that could offset some welfare loss.

items.title: Kenya diagnostic identifies $1.5 billion in potential investment across three sectors
items.summary: A country private-sector diagnostic estimates that reforms and complementary public investment in fruit value chains, coastal tourism, and medical-consumables manufacturing could unlock up to $1.5 billion in incremental private investment and 80,000 direct jobs with higher earnings. It also records broad constraints: 75 percent of surveyed firms report frequent power outages, while private credit fell from 36.7 percent of GDP in 2015 to 29.1 percent in 2024. The investment and employment figures are scenario estimates.

items.title: Tanzania’s growth is strengthening, but formal firms and productive jobs remain scarce
items.summary: The 2026 Tanzania Economic Update estimates 5.9 percent growth in 2025 and projects 6.1 percent in 2026, while warning that government spending accounted for more than two-thirds of last year’s real GDP growth. Its jobs analysis finds employment is widespread but often informal and low-productivity; only 12 percent of registered firms are young, compared with 38 percent in Rwanda. The projections are conditional and the report identifies meaningful downside risks.

items.title: A national employer survey locates Saudi skill gaps in higher-value sectors
items.publisher: World Bank and Saudi Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development
items.summary: A survey of more than 3,000 private establishments, weighted for national analysis, finds employers reporting cognitive, socio-behavioral, and technical skill imbalances. Gaps are especially pronounced in information technology, manufacturing, and services, and among mature, exporting, and highly skilled firms—the businesses most closely tied to diversification. Because the evidence is employer-reported, it measures perceived shortages and mismatches rather than independently tested worker competency, but it offers unusually granular sector and firm-size comparisons.

items.title: Somalia’s financial-governance gains face aid cuts and rising fiscal pressure
items.publisher: World Bank and Federal Government of Somalia
items.summary: Somalia’s 2025 Financial Governance Report records progress in petroleum agreements, concession oversight, and financial-sector supervision. It also flags a harsher fiscal setting shaped by reduced foreign aid, rising security costs, a growing wage bill, and drought risk. The committee further identifies unclear rules for public-property transactions and new public-private agreements that may escape concession oversight. This is an official governance assessment, useful both for its documented reforms and for the risks its authors choose to foreground.

items.title: A proposed Thailand–Malaysia corridor pairs trade integration with conflict-sensitive development
items.geography: Southern Thailand and northern Peninsular Malaysia
items.summary: An inception report frames a cross-border economic corridor around stark regional gaps: Thailand’s conflict-affected southern provinces contain 2.7 percent of the national population but generate 0.7 percent of GDP, with productivity below one-third of the national rate. The planned work combines research, consultations, and bilateral dialogue on trade, investment, and connectivity. Because this is a project blueprint, its development benefits remain prospective; its value is the integration of economic planning with peace-building and local participation.
